newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Argentine official plays down trade spat with U.S..
newsitem.headline: Argentine official plays down trade spat with U.S..

text.p: Washington's removal of trade benefits to Argentina because of a spat over patent protection was no surprise and would affect American business interests as much as Argentine, an Argentine official said Wednesday.

Jorge Campbell, secretary of international economic relations at the Argentine Foreign Ministry, said the sanctions followed a "legal process" and that political and economic relations between the two countries remained excellent.

"In fact, it is something...that follows a legal process. It was no surprise," Campbell told reporters in Rio de Janeiro where deputy trade ministers from 34 countries in the region were discussing the setting up a Free Trade Area of the Americas (FTAA).
Campbell said the measure potentially affected $260 million of Argentine exports and meant some products would become more expensive for U.S. importers.
"The withdrawal of preference also affects U.S. interests," he said.
In Buenos Aires, the mood was somewhat angrier. An official said today Argentina would look into an appeal of the U.S. move before the World Trade Organization.
Argentine Foreign Minister Guido Di Tella last night slammed the U.S. action as "unnecessary and arbitrary".
President Bill Clinton signed an order Tuesday slashing by 50 percent the number of goods that can be imported duty-free from Argentina, citing "inadequate" intellectual property laws.

"In any case, the political relations between Argentina and the United States are excellent," Campbell said, noting that Americans were the largest foreign investors in Argentina and a significant trade partner.
"Zero, absolutely zero," he added when questioned about the impact of the issue on the atmosphere of the FTAA talks in Rio.
